title: KAKE NEWS INVESTIGATES: Duplicate license plate numbers lead to dangerous situations for some Kansas drivers

reading.body:
This is a false-match failure in an automated license plate reader. The system compares the letters and numbers on a plate and nothing else, so a KU Alumni plate reading 7007 and a stolen vehicle's temporary tag reading 7007 are the same hit. The failure sits at the alerting stage, before any officer sees the vehicle: the camera flags a possible stolen vehicle and the stop follows from that flag. A Wichita police captain is quoted saying the cameras read only letters and numbers, not plate types, which is why a specialty plate cannot be told apart from another design.

Catching it would have required the system to read the plate background as well as its characters, which the reporting says police have only discussed training the AI to do. It would also have required a numbering scheme without duplicates, and Kansas is described as moving from six digit to seven digit numbers that are not duplicated. In the Colwich stop, an officer's own recognition of the minivan was what corrected the alert. In the Catoosa stop, no such check intervened before police stopped the couple at gunpoint and handcuffed Matthew.

What is not established is fault. The account comes from a single outlet's investigation, and it reports no finding against Flock or against either department. The training of the AI to recognise plate backgrounds is described as a discussion, not a change that was made, and the shift to seven digit numbers is reported as a move in progress.

reports.title: KAKE NEWS INVESTIGATES: Duplicate license plate numbers lead to dangerous situations for some Kansas drivers

summary:
Matthew and Leah Spurlock were repeatedly pulled over because their Kansas KU Alumni license plate number, 7007, matched a stolen GMC pickup's temporary tag. In Colwich, Kansas, a Flock camera alerted police to a possible stolen vehicle, but an officer recognized their minivan and learned the stolen plate had the same number with a different background. About a month later in Catoosa, Oklahoma, another Flock camera led police to stop them at gunpoint, handcuff Matthew, and question them before the mistake was sorted out.

Wichita police Captain Casey Slaughter said Flock cameras read only letters and numbers, not plate types, so they cannot tell a specialty plate from another design. Kansas has more than 100 plate designs, about half specialty, and the state duplicates numbers. The article says Kansas is moving from six digit to seven digit plate numbers that are not duplicated. Wichita police have discussed training Flock's AI to recognize plate backgrounds. The Spurlocks' stolen vehicle entry has expired, so they no longer expect stops, and they hope to keep their 14 year old plate.
